title: Deterministic control of the probabilistic phase dynamics in injection-locked spin-torque nano-oscillators
authors: Abderrazak Hakam, Chloé Chopin, Nhat-Tan Phan, Nicolas Mollard, Franck Badets, Louis Hutin, Luana Benetti, Alex S. Jenkins, Ricardo Ferreira, Ursula Ebels, Philippe Talatchian
abstract: Spin-torque nano-oscillators (STNOs) inherently exhibit thermally driven phase fluctuations that render their dynamics truly stochastic. Here, we demonstrate that, despite this intrinsic randomness, the probability of occupying each phase state can be deterministically and continuously programmed. We experimentally investigate a vortex-based STNO operating under second-harmonic injection-locking, where the oscillator phase settles into two degenerate attractors separated by $π$ and undergoes thermally activated phase jumps. By applying a weak radio-frequency perturbation at the free-running frequency, we tune the phase-jump rates between the two attractors without suppressing the fluctuations, achieving continuous probability control from the unbiased limit to values approaching 0 or 1. The bias phase selects which attractor is favored while the bias amplitude sets the strength of the imbalance, providing two complementary control knobs within a single nanoscale device. A phase-reduced description based on an effective quasipotential quantitatively accounts for the observations. These results establish injection-locked STNOs as programmable stochastic elements and provide a hardware primitive for probabilistic computing, Ising machines, and brain-inspired computing architectures.
summary: The research demonstrates that intrinsic thermal noise in spin-torque nano-oscillators can be deterministically controlled by applying an external radio-frequency bias. By tuning the phase and amplitude of this bias, researchers can program the probability of the oscillator settling into one of two metastable phase states. This establishes STNOs as tunable stochastic elements suitable for next-generation probabilistic computing architectures.
main_problem: The goal is to deterministically control the probability of occupying different phase states in Spin-Torque Nano-Oscillators (STNOs) despite their inherent thermal stochasticity.
main_result: By applying a weak RF bias perturbation, the symmetry of the system's quasipotential can be broken, allowing for continuous programming of the occupation probability between two metastable phase states from unbiased to near 0 or 1.
method: The study uses experimental measurements of voltage-time traces and analyzes the resulting stochastic jumps using Markov process theory applied to a reduced phase description.
model_or_system: The physical system is a vortex-based STNO operating under second-harmonic injection-locking (SHIL). The dynamics are modeled by an effective quasipotential $V(\Delta\phi)$ derived from the underlying spin dynamics, which governs thermally activated jumps between $\Delta\phi=0$ and $\Delta\phi=\pi$.
key_observables: Occupation probabilities ($P_0, P_\pi$), mean dwell times ($\tau_0, \tau_\pi$), and the phase difference $\Delta\phi$.
important_parameters: Bias phase ($\alpha$) and bias amplitude/power ($P_{\text{bias}}$) are the primary control knobs; temperature ($T$) governs thermal fluctuations.
main_assumptions: The dynamics can be accurately described by a two-state Markov process governed by an effective quasipotential, and that first-order perturbation theory is sufficient for modeling the bias effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic setups (Fig. 1), qualitative changes in the quasipotential from symmetric to tilted potentials (Fig. 1b), and time traces/histograms demonstrating how varying the bias phase ($\alpha$) or power ($P_{\text{bias}}$) controls state occupation probabilities (e.g., Fig. 3, Fig. 5).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the inherent stochasticity of STNOs to introducing an RF bias control mechanism. It details the theoretical modeling using quasipotentials and then presents experimental measurements showing how tuning the bias parameters allows for deterministic programming of the system's probabilistic state.
why_interesting: This work provides a solid physical realization of programmable stochastic elements, linking fundamental concepts from non-equilibrium statistical mechanics (metastable states, barrier crossing rates) to tangible hardware primitives for computation.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) Schematic of the experimental implementation. A vortex-based STNO is driven into auto-oscillation at fre- quency f0 by a DC current IDC and a static mostly out-of- plane magnetic field HDC. An RF drive at fIL ≈2f0 is used for second-harmonic injection-locking, and a weaker RF bias excitation at fbias ≈f0 is applied.(b) Qualitative quasipoten- tial for the phase difference ∆ϕ. Under the SHIL drive alone, the quasipotential is symmetric, with two equivalent minima at 0 and π (black). The RF bias adds a phase-dependent con- tribution (green), yielding a tilted quasipotential (blue) with unequal transition barriers.

FIG. 2. Experimental circuit schematic. A DC current source injects a constant current into the STNO, induc- ing vortex-core auto-oscillations at frequency f0. Second- harmonic injection-locking is achieved by applying an RF voltage at fIL ≈2f0 through a bias tee. An RF bias exci- tation at fbias ≈f0 is applied to a field-line fabricated above the device, generating a local in-plane RF magnetic field that influences the vortex-core dynamics.
